claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant impact on delivery of NHS care.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant impact on delivery of NHS care.
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Moynihan et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2022; Mansfield et al., 2021; Fisher, 2023a) in the Introduction section.

claim: The OpenSAFELY Service Restoration Observatory (SRO) was developed to develop key measures of primary care activity and describe the trends in these measures throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: We have developed the OpenSAFELY Service Restoration Observatory (SRO) to develop key measures of primary care activity and describe the trends in these measures throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's purpose and methods.

claim: The study analyzed primary care electronic health record (EHR) data on 48 million adults.
source: we developed an open source software framework for data management and analysis to describe trends and variation in clinical activity across primary care electronic health record (EHR) data on 48 million adults.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study population size.

claim: SNOMED-CT codelists were developed for key measures of primary care clinical activity such as blood pressure monitoring and asthma reviews.
source: We developed SNOMED-CT codelists for key measures of primary care clinical activity such as blood pressure monitoring and asthma reviews, selected by an expert clinical advisory group
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study period was January 2019-December 2021.
source: conducted a population cohort-based study to describe trends and variation in these measures January 2019-December 2021
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study timeframe.

claim: 11 measures reflective of clinical activity in general practice were produced.
source: We produced 11 measures reflective of clinical activity in general practice.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study output.

claim: A substantial drop in activity was observed in all measures at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: A substantial drop in activity was observed in all measures at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: By April 2021, the median rate had recovered to within 15% of the median rate in April 2019 in six measures.
source: By April 2021, the median rate had recovered to within 15% of the median rate in April 2019 in six measures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: The remaining measures showed a sustained drop, ranging from a 18.5% reduction in medication reviews to a 42.0% reduction in blood pressure monitoring.
source: The remaining measures showed a sustained drop, ranging from a 18.5% reduction in medication reviews to a 42.0% reduction in blood pressure monitoring.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Three measures continued to show a sustained drop by December 2021.
source: Three measures continued to show a sustained drop by December 2021.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Some clinical activities such as cardiovascular disease assessment were not restored to near normal levels by December 2020.
source: Following the first wave in March 2020, we found that some clinical activities such as cardiovascular disease assessment were not restored to near normal levels by December 2020 as was anticipated in guidance issued by NHS England in July 2020 (NHS England, 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: OpenSAFELY is a secure analytics platform for electronic patient records built on behalf of NHS England to deliver urgent academic and operational research during the pandemic.
source: OpenSAFELY is a secure analytics platform for electronic patient records built by our group on behalf of NHS England to deliver urgent academic and operational research during the pandemic.
evidence: This is a description of the platform used in the study.

claim: OpenSAFELY allows analysis of medical diagnoses, clinical tests, prescriptions, as well as demographic details such as age, sex, ethnicity, making detailed subgroup analysis possible.
source: Using regularly updated data, it allows analysis of medical diagnoses, clinical tests, prescriptions, as well as demographic details such as age, sex, ethnicity, making detailed subgroup analysis possible.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the OpenSAFELY platform.

claim: Through linkage of other data sources, OpenSAFELY provides information such as hospital admissions, registered deaths or COVID-19 testing data.
source: Through linkage of other data sources, it also provides information such as hospital admissions, registered deaths or COVID-19 testing data.
evidence: This describes the data linkage capabilities of OpenSAFELY.

claim: Initial work was performed using data available in OpenSAFELY-TPP, covering 40% of all general practices in England.
source: This initial work was performed using data available in OpenSAFELY-TPP, covering 40% of all general practices in England.
evidence: This describes the scope of previous work.

claim: The OpenSAFELY platform has been extended to both major EHR vendors in England, TPP and EMIS, allowing federated analyses and dashboards to be executed across the full primary care records for all patients registered at 99% of England's practices.
source: We have since extended the OpenSAFELY platform to both major EHR vendors in England, TPP and EMIS, allowing federated analyses and dashboards to be executed across the full primary care records for all patients registered at 99% of England's practices.
evidence: This describes the expansion of the platform.

claim: The study included all adult patients (n=48,352,770) who were alive and registered with a TPP or EMIS general practice (n=6389 practices) in England at the beginning of each month between January 2019 and December 2021.
source: We included all adult patients (n=48,352,770) who were alive and registered with a TPP or EMIS general practice (n=6389 practices) in England at the beginning of each month between January 2019 and December 2021.
evidence: This describes the study population.

claim: All coded events in each month for each monthly cohort were included.
source: All coded events in each month for each monthly cohort were included.
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: Demographic variables identified for patients included age, sex, region of their practice address, index of multiple deprivation (IMD) and ethnicity.
source: We also identified demographic variables for these patients including age, sex, region of their practice address, index of multiple deprivation (IMD) and ethnicity.
evidence: This describes the demographic data collected.

claim: A clinical advisory group was convened made up of front-line general practitioner and pharmacists; national clinical advisors and pathology leads; and clinical and research staff from the Bennett Institute.
source: In order to develop key measures of NHS clinical activity we convened a clinical advisory group made up of: front-line general practitioner and pharmacists; national clinical advisors and pathology leads; and clinical and research staff from the Bennett Institute.
evidence: This describes the composition of the advisory group.

claim: The clinical advisory group manually reviewed charts representing coding of clinical activity.
source: This group manually reviewed charts representing coding of clinical activity the development of which we have described in detail elsewhere (Curtis et al., 2022b; Curtis et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the methodology, with reference to previous publications.

claim: The CTV3 terminology coding hierarchy was used to produce a large number of charts indicating variation in clinical coding activity between practices across a range of clinical areas.
source: Briefly, we used the CTV3 terminology coding hierarchy (the coding system available in OpenSAFELY-TPP at the time) to produce a large number of charts indicating variation in clinical coding activity between practices across a range of clinical areas.
evidence: This describes the methodology used.

claim: The clinical advisory group was asked to suggest key measures for each clinical area considering the following criteria: high volume usage, clinically relevant to front-line practice and whether they are more widely indicative of other problems in service delivery across the NHS.
source: The clinical advisory group was asked to suggest key measures for each clinical area considering the following criteria: high volume usage, clinically relevant to front-line practice and whether they are more widely indicative of other problems in service delivery across the NHS (for example a decrease in records for blood tests for kidney function may be a true drop in GPs requesting these tests or it may be related to delays in laboratories processing the results).
evidence: This describes the criteria used for measure selection.

claim: Blood pressure monitoring is a commonly-used assessment used to identify patients with hypertension or to ensure optimal treatment for those with known hypertension.
source: A commonly-used assessment used to identify patients with hypertension or to ensure optimal treatment for those with known hypertension.
evidence: This is a description of the clinical purpose of blood pressure monitoring.

claim: Blood pressure monitoring helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long-term risks of complications from hypertension such as stroke, myocardial infarction and kidney disease.
source: This helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long-term risks of complications from hypertension such as stroke, myocardial infarction and kidney disease.
evidence: This describes the clinical rationale for blood pressure monitoring.

claim: Cardiovascular Disease 10 Year Risk Assessment is a commonly-used risk assessment used to identify patients with an increased risk of cardiovascular events in the next 10 years.
source: A commonly-used risk assessment used to identify patients with an increased risk of cardiovascular events in the next 10 years. QRISK3, 2018
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of CVD risk assessment.

claim: Cardiovascular Disease 10 Year Risk Assessment helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long term risks of complications such as stroke or myocardial infarction.
source: This helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long term risks of complications such as stroke or myocardial infarction.
evidence: This describes the clinical rationale for CVD risk assessment.

claim: Cholesterol testing is a commonly-used blood test used as part of a routine cardiovascular disease 10-year risk assessment and also to identify patients with lipid disorders (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia).
source: A commonly-used blood test used as part of a routine cardiovascular disease 10-year risk assessment QRISK3, 2018 and also to identify patients with lipid disorders (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia).
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of cholesterol testing.

claim: Cholesterol testing helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long term risks of complications such as stroke or myocardial infarction.
source: This helps ensure appropriate treatment, with the aim of reducing long term risks of complications such as stroke or myocardial infarction.
evidence: This describes the clinical rationale for cholesterol testing.

claim: An ALT blood test is one of a group of liver function tests (LFTs) which are used to detect problems with the function of the liver.
source: An ALT blood test is one of a group of liver function tests (LFTs) which are used to detect problems with the function of the liver.
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of ALT testing.

claim: ALT is often used to monitor patients on medications which may affect the liver or which rely on the liver to break them down within the body.
source: It is often used to monitor patients on medications which may affect the liver or which rely on the liver to break them down within the body.
evidence: This describes a clinical use of ALT testing.

claim: ALT tests are also tested for patients with known or suspected liver dysfunction.
source: They are also tested for patients with known or suspected liver dysfunction.
evidence: This describes a clinical use of ALT testing.

claim: TSH is used for the diagnosis and monitoring of hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, including making changes to thyroid replacement therapy dosing.
source: TSH is used for the diagnosis and monitoring of hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, including making changes to thyroid replacement therapy dosing.
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of TSH testing.

claim: RBC is completed as part of a group of tests referred to as a full blood count (FBC), used to detect a variety of disorders of the blood, such as anaemia and infection.
source: RBC is completed as part of a group of tests referred to as a full blood count (FBC), used to detect a variety of disorders of the blood, such as anaemia and infection.
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of RBC testing.

claim: HbA1c is a long term indicator of diabetes control.
source: HbA1c is a long term indicator of diabetes control.
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of HbA1c testing.

claim: NICE guidelines recommend that individuals with diabetes have their HbA1c measured at least twice a year.
source: NICE guidelines recommend that individuals with diabetes have their HbA1c measured at least twice a year. NICE, 2015
evidence: This is supported by citation to NICE guidelines.

claim: Poor diabetic control can place individuals living with diabetes at an increased risk of the complications of diabetes.
source: Poor diabetic control can place individuals living with diabetes at an increased risk of the complications of diabetes.
evidence: This is based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Sodium is completed as part of a group of tests referred to as a renal profile, used to detect a variety of disorders of the kidneys.
source: Sodium is completed as part of a group of tests referred to as a renal profile, used to detect a variety of disorders of the kidneys.
evidence: This describes the clinical purpose of sodium testing.

claim: A renal profile is also often used to monitor patients on medications which may affect the kidneys or which rely on the kidneys to remove them from the body.
source: A renal profile is also often used to monitor patients on medications which may affect the kidneys or which rely on the kidneys to remove them from the body.
evidence: This describes a clinical use of renal function testing.

claim: The British Thoracic Society and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network on the management of asthma recommend that people with asthma receive a review of their condition at least annually.
source: The British Thoracic Society and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network on the management of asthma recommend that people with asthma receive a review of their condition at least annually.
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical guidelines (British Thoracic Society, 2021).

claim: If a patient with asthma has not been reviewed, it is possible that their asthma control may have worsened, leading to a greater chance of symptoms and admission to hospital.
source: If a patient has not been reviewed, it is possible that their asthma control may have worsened, leading to a greater chance of symptoms and admission to hospital.
evidence: This is based on clinical reasoning and inference.

claim: NICE recommends that all individuals living with COPD have an annual review with the exception of individuals living with very severe (stage 4) COPD being reviewed at least twice a year.
source: It is recommended by NICE that all individuals living with COPD have an annual review with the exception of individuals living with very severe (stage 4) COPD being reviewed at least twice a year. NICE, 2018
evidence: This is supported by citation to NICE guidelines.

claim: If a patient with COPD has not been reviewed, it is possible that their COPD control may have worsened, leading to a greater chance of symptoms and admission to hospital.
source: If a patient has not been reviewed, it is possible that their COPD control may have worsened, leading to a greater chance of symptoms and admission to hospital.
evidence: This is based on clinical reasoning and inference.

claim: Many medicines are used long-term and they should be reviewed regularly to ensure they are still safe, effective and appropriate.
source: Many medicines are used long-term and they should be reviewed regularly to ensure they are still safe, effective and appropriate.
evidence: This is based on established clinical practice.

claim: Medication review is a broad term ranging from a notes-led review without a patient, to an in-depth Structured Medication Review with multiple appointments and follow-up.
source: Medication review is a broad term ranging from a notes-led review without a patient, to an in-depth Structured Medication Review with multiple appointments and follow-up.
evidence: This describes the scope of medication review activities.

claim: For each key measure of activity, a single codelist was developed using the SNOMED-CT coding system.
source: For each key measure of activity, working with the clinical advisory group,we used the SNOMED-CT coding system, as the mandated NHS standard, to develop a single codelist (Table 1), which can be deployed across any system using SNOMED-CT.
evidence: This describes the methodology for codelist development.

claim: Where a well-defined nationally curated codelist existed, such as Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF), the codelist released by NHS Digital was used.
source: Where a well-defined nationally curated codelist existed, such as Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF), we used the codelist released by NHS Digital (NHS Digital, 2020a).
evidence: This describes the methodology for codelist selection.

claim: For pathology testing measures with no NHS mandated codelists, SNOMED-CT codes were searched using OpenCodelists.
source: For pathology testing measures with no NHS mandated codelists, we searched for SNOMED-CT codes using OpenCodelists.
evidence: This describes the methodology for codelist development.

claim: For each measure, the monthly rate of coding activity per 1000 registered adults was calculated for each practice.
source: For each measure, we calculated the monthly rate of coding activity per 1000 registered adults for each practice.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Where multiple codes from a single codelist are recorded in the patient record in a single month only a single record will be returned.
source: Where multiple codes from a single codelist are recorded in the patient record in a single month only a single record will be returned.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Practices not recording a single instance of a relevant code in each codelist across the entire study period were excluded from further analysis.
source: We excluded practices not recording a single instance of a relevant code in each codelist across the entire study period from further analysis;as all the measures analysed here are high volume, any practices with zero recorded events for a measure are likely atypical.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology with reasoning.

claim: The median and deciles of coding activity rates across all practices each month were calculated.
source: We then calculated the median and deciles of coding activity rates across all practices each month.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: The change in coding activity was classified using the median rate in April 2020 and 2021 compared to April 2019 which was defined as the 'baseline'.
source: For each key measure chart, we classified the change in coding activity using the median rate in April 2020 and 2021 compared to April 2019 which we defined as the 'baseline'.
evidence: This describes the methodology for classification.

claim: April was identified as the first full month of a full 'lockdown' in England in 2020 and additionally had 20 business days in 2019, 2020, and 2021, allowing fair comparison.
source: April was identified as the first full month of a full 'lockdown' in England in 2020 and additionally had 20 business days in 2019, 2020, and 2021, allowing fair comparison.
evidence: This provides the rationale for selecting April as the comparison month.

claim: Data management and analysis was performed using the OpenSAFELY software libraries and Python, both implemented using Python 3.8.
source: Data management and analysis was performed using the OpenSAFELY software libraries and Python, both implemented using Python 3.8 with all code shared openly for review and reuse github.com/opensafely/SRO-Measures.
evidence: This describes the software used for analysis.

claim: All codelists used are openly available for inspection and re-use at OpenSAFELY Codelists.
source: All codelists used are openly available for inspection and re-use at OpenSAFELY Codelists (Open Codelists, 2020).
evidence: This describes the availability of study materials.

claim: The analysis was delivered using federated analysis through the OpenSAFELY platform.
source: This analysis was delivered using federated analysis through the OpenSAFELY platform: codelists and code for data management and data analysis were specified once using the OpenSAFELY tools; then transmitted securely to the OpenSAFELY-TPP platform within TPP's secure environment, and separately to the OpenSAFELY-EMIS platform within EMIS's secure environment, where they were each executed separately against local patient data; summary results were then reviewed for disclosiveness, released, and combined for the final outputs.
evidence: This describes the federated analysis methodology.

claim: The study included 48,352,770 registered adult patients across 6389 practices, >98% of total practices in England.
source: Our study included 48,352,770 registered adult patients across 6389 practices, >98% of total practices in England.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the study population.

claim: From January 2019 to December 2021, 447 million recorded events were identified across the 11 key measures.
source: From January 2019 to December 2021 we identified 447 million recorded events across the 11 key measures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: The number of patients included from January 2019 to December 2021 ranged from 1.16 million for the COPD review measure to 27.77 million patients for the blood pressure monitoring measure.
source: The number of patients included from January 2019 to December 2021 ranged from 1.16 million for the COPD review measure to 27.77 million patients for the blood pressure monitoring measure, representing 2.60 million and 79.30 million coded events, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: The median practice level rate per 1000 registered patients at baseline ranged from 1.10 in COPD reviews to 65.03 in blood pressure monitoring.
source: The median practice level rate per 1000 registered patients at baseline ranged from 1.10 in COPD reviews to 65.03 in blood pressure monitoring.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: In April 2020, for all measures the median dropped substantially compared to April 2019, ranging from a 91.75% reduction in cholesterol tests to a 36.42% reduction in medication reviews.
source: In April 2020, for all measures the median dropped substantially compared to April 2019, ranging from a 91.75% reduction in cholesterol tests (23.99–1.98 recorded codes per 1000 registered patients) to a 36.42% reduction in medication reviews (34.10–21.68 recorded codes per 1000 registered patients; Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: By April 2021, the change in the median compared with April 2019 ranged from a decrease of 42.03% in blood pressure monitoring to a decrease of 1.65% in thyroid testing.
source: By April 2021, the change in the median compared with April 2019 ranged from a decrease of 42.03% in blood pressure monitoring (April 2019: 65.03, April 2021: 37.70) to a decrease of 1.65% in thyroid testing (April 2019: 23.65, April 2021: 23.26).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: By April 2021 activity in all six blood monitoring measures had 'recovered' to within 15% of baseline, based on the simple SRO classification system.
source: By April 2021 activity in all six blood monitoring measures had 'recovered' to within 15% of baseline, based on the simple SRO classification system.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Reviews for asthma and COPD experienced reductions of 39.89% and 72.73% in 2020, respectively.
source: Reviews for asthma and COPD experienced reductions of 39.89% and 72.73% in 2020, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Reductions in asthma and COPD reviews were sustained in 2021 with rates of 2.76 (-23.55% from baseline) and 0.77 (-30.00% from baseline) in asthma and COPD, respectively.
source: These reductions were sustained in 2021 with rates of 2.76 (-23.55% from baseline) and 0.77 (-30.00% from baseline) in asthma and COPD, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Blood pressure monitoring and assessment of cardiovascular 10-year risk were classified with rates dropping by 42.03% and 37.74% between April 2019 and April 2021.
source: Blood pressure monitoring and assessment of cardiovascular 10-year risk were also classified with rates dropping by 42.03% and 37.74% between April 2019 and April 2021.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Most measures show a similar pattern, a steady rate with wide variation prior to the pandemic with a steep decline in April 2020 during the national lockdown, followed by partial or full recovery over the summer of 2020 and into 2021.
source: Most measures show a similar pattern, a steady rate with wide variation prior to the pandemic with a steep decline in April 2020 during the national lockdown, followed by partial or full recovery over the summer of 2020 and into 2021.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Blood pressure monitoring, cardiovascular disease risk assessment and medication reviews continued to show a sustained drop as of December 2021.
source: Blood pressure monitoring, cardiovascular disease risk assessment and medication reviews continued to show a sustained drop as of December 2021.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Blood tests (renal function assessment, cholesterol testing, liver function testing, thyroid function testing, full blood count and glycated haemoglobin) all show a temporary decrease in rates in September 2021.
source: Blood tests (renal function assessment, cholesterol testing, liver function testing, thyroid function testing, full blood count and glycated haemoglobin) all show a temporary decrease in rates in September 2021.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The temporary decrease in blood test rates in September 2021 is likely to be a consequence of a shortage of blood specimen collecting tubes rather than a result of the pandemic.
source: This is likely to be a consequence of a shortage of blood specimen collecting tubes rather than a result of the pandemic, with national guidance to temporarily halt non-clinically urgent blood tests (DHSC & NHS England and Improvement, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to national guidance.

claim: The OpenSAFELY platform allows federated analysis to be run across the full dataset of all raw, single-event-level clinical events for 57.9 million patients.
source: The OpenSAFELY platform allows federated analysis to be run across the full dataset of all raw, single-event-level clinical events for 57.9 million patients; all patients registered at 99% of all general practices in England.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the OpenSAFELY platform.

claim: OpenSAFELY can provide data in near-real time, providing unprecedented opportunities for audit and feedback to rapidly identify and resolve concerns around health service activity.
source: OpenSAFELY can provide data in near-real time, providing unprecedented opportunities for audit and feedback to rapidly identify and resolve concerns around health service activity.
evidence: This describes the capabilities and implications of the OpenSAFELY platform.

claim: The delay from occurrence of a clinical event to it appearing in the OpenSAFELY platform varies from 2 to 9 days.
source: We choose when to update the data, and currently update on a weekly basis, meaning the the delay from occurrence of a clinical event to it appearing in the OpenSAFELY platform varies from 2 to 9 days.
evidence: This describes the data update frequency of the OpenSAFELY platform.

claim: OpenSAFELY is substantially faster than any other source of GP data, including those giving much less complete records.
source: This is substantially faster than any other source of GP data, including those giving much less complete records.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about OpenSAFELY's performance.

claim: OpenSAFELY has already been used to understand disease risk.
source: OpenSAFELY has already been used to understand disease risk (Williamson et al., 2020), monitor vaccination coverage (Curtis et al., 2022a; Parker et al., 2023) and novel treatments (Green et al., 2023), assess patient safety (Fisher et al., 2022), inform public health guidance and policy and much more (NCBI, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OpenSAFELY has been used to monitor vaccination coverage.
source: OpenSAFELY has already been used to understand disease risk (Williamson et al., 2020), monitor vaccination coverage (Curtis et al., 2022a; Parker et al., 2023) and novel treatments (Green et al., 2023), assess patient safety (Fisher et al., 2022), inform public health guidance and policy and much more (NCBI, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OpenSAFELY has been used to monitor novel treatments.
source: OpenSAFELY has already been used to understand disease risk (Williamson et al., 2020), monitor vaccination coverage (Curtis et al., 2022a; Parker et al., 2023) and novel treatments (Green et al., 2023), assess patient safety (Fisher et al., 2022), inform public health guidance and policy and much more (NCBI, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OpenSAFELY has been used to assess patient safety.
source: OpenSAFELY has already been used to understand disease risk (Williamson et al., 2020), monitor vaccination coverage (Curtis et al., 2022a; Parker et al., 2023) and novel treatments (Green et al., 2023), assess patient safety (Fisher et al., 2022), inform public health guidance and policy and much more (NCBI, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Coded activity may not reflect the true scale and breadth of activity.
source: With the exception of a small amount of legally restricted data, all occurrences of clinical codes are included, however coded activity may not reflect the true scale and breadth of activity.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Codes recorded in general practice do not necessarily indicate unique or new events.
source: Codes recorded in general practice do not necessarily indicate unique or new events; for example one patient encounter could generate several similar codes, one patient might have similar diagnoses recorded multiple times over time, or practices might bulk-import information.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: For each measure, no more than one coded event per patient per calendar month is counted.
source: For each measure, we count no more than one coded event per patient per calendar month, which avoids overcounting where practices use multiple codes to describe a single encounter, but will not account for genuine multiple encounters in a single calendar month.
evidence: This describes the methodology and its limitations.

claim: For some of the key measures reflecting routine testing, only test results returned to GPs are included.
source: For some of the key measures reflecting routine testing, only test results returned to GPs are included, which will usually exclude tests requested while a person is in hospital and other settings like a private clinic.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The key measures developed are not exhaustive and some important clinical areas are not covered, including mental health and female and reproductive health.
source: The key measures developed are not exhaustive and some important clinical areas are not covered, including mental health and female and reproductive health.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: It can be difficult to capture clinical activity in some areas due to incomplete coding or care spanning different services such as community trusts.
source: We have discussed the reasons for these omissions previously (Curtis et al., 2023), but briefly, it can be difficult to capture clinical activity in some areas due to incomplete coding or care spanning different services such as community trusts.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, with reference to previous work.

claim: A 15% window around the pre-pandemic baseline was chosen as a pragmatic cutoff to highlight changes in service restoration.
source: A 15% window around the pre-pandemic baseline was chosen as a pragmatic cutoff to highlight these changes.
evidence: This describes the methodology for classification.

claim: Recovery to the pre-pandemic baseline may not always be expected or appropriate.
source: We accept that recovery to the pre-pandemic baseline may not always be expected or appropriate.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the classification system.

claim: The measures only capture key measures of clinical activity which do not reflect all clinical care carried out by practices, administrative activity, referral, liaison with other services and other services delivered by general practice.
source: Finally we are only capturing key measures of clinical activity which do not reflect all clinical care carried out by practices, administrative activity, referral, liaison with other services and other services delivered by general practice.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The WHO found 94% of 135 countries reported some kind of disruption to health services as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The disruption to health services as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic has been felt globally, with the WHO finding 94% of 135 countries reported some kind of disruption and 48% reported >5% disruption to primary care (World Health Organisation, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: 48% of countries reported >5% disruption to primary care as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The disruption to health services as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic has been felt globally, with the WHO finding 94% of 135 countries reported some kind of disruption and 48% reported >5% disruption to primary care (World Health Organisation, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: A systematic review of utilisation of healthcare services during the pandemic reported a 37% reduction in services overall across 20 countries.
source: Similarly, a systematic review of utilisation of healthcare services during the pandemic reported a 37% reduction in services overall across p20 countries (Moynihan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: A study in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) of primary care contacts for physical and mental health in the UK showed a considerable drop in activity as a result of national restrictions which only partly recovered by July 2020.
source: A study in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) of primary care contacts for physical and mental health in the UK showed a considerable drop in activity as a result of national restrictions which only partly recovered by July 2020 (Mansfield et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the winter of 2021 NHS Digital reported that general practice delivered 34.6 million appointments representing a 26% increase (7.1 million appointments) in November 2021 compared to pre-pandemic.
source: Despite changes in evaluated clinical activity, in the winter of 2021 NHS Digital reported that general practice delivered 34.6 million appointments representing a 26% increase (7.1 million appointments) in November 2021 compared to pre-pandemic (NHS Digital, 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to NHS Digital data.

claim: Decreases in clinical activity may reflect appropriate prioritisation of other clinical activity.
source: However we believe the following broad points may help aid interpretation. Our measures reflect only a few areas of high volume clinical activity; decreases may reflect appropriate prioritisation of other clinical activity as we have found with INR tests (Curtis et al., 2022b) or the delivery of COVID-19 vaccinations (NHS England, 2021b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Reduced clinical activity can be explained by changes in guidance and financial incentives.
source: We have previously described how reduced clinical activity can be explained by changes in guidance and financial incentives (Curtis et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NHS Health Checks were paused during the pandemic.
source: For example NHS Health Checks, which are used to detect early signs of high blood pressure, heart disease or type 2 diabetes, were paused during the pandemic; this is likely to explain the sustained drop in activity in cardiovascular disease risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring (Office for Health Improvement & Disparities, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to official guidance.

claim: The pause in NHS Health Checks is likely to explain the sustained drop in activity in cardiovascular disease risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring.
source: For example NHS Health Checks, which are used to detect early signs of high blood pressure, heart disease or type 2 diabetes, were paused during the pandemic; this is likely to explain the sustained drop in activity in cardiovascular disease risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring (Office for Health Improvement & Disparities, 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pause in NHS Health Checks.

claim: Home monitoring of blood pressure may not be recorded completely or consistently in GP records.
source: However, in specific cases, this may reflect changes in the style of delivery of a clinical activity, rather than the volume: for example, where patients record their own blood pressure at home since, as we have previously highlighted, home monitoring of blood pressure may not be recorded completely or consistently in GP records.
evidence: This is an inference about potential recording issues.

claim: Not all reductions in clinical activity should be interpreted as problematic.
source: In addition, not all reductions should be interpreted as problematic: as part of the COVID-19 recovery, health systems are aiming to be more resilient, responsive and sustainable (Durski et al., 2020); complete recovery may not always be appropriate and reductions in clinical activity across some domains may reflect rational reprioritisation of activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Health systems are aiming to be more resilient, responsive and sustainable as part of the COVID-19 recovery.
source: In addition, not all reductions should be interpreted as problematic: as part of the COVID-19 recovery, health systems are aiming to be more resilient, responsive and sustainable (Durski et al., 2020); complete recovery may not always be appropriate and reductions in clinical activity across some domains may reflect rational reprioritisation of activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Complete recovery to pre-pandemic levels may not always be appropriate and reductions in clinical activity across some domains may reflect rational reprioritisation of activity.
source: complete recovery may not always be appropriate and reductions in clinical activity across some domains may reflect rational reprioritisation of activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Data analyses such as this may help to rapidly identify the pragmatic changes in prioritisation being made by individual dispersed organisations or people across the healthcare ecosystem before those changes are explicitly surfaced or discussed through other mechanisms.
source: Where these changes in priority have not been nationally planned, data analyses such as ours may help to rapidly identify the pragmatic changes in prioritisation being made by individual dispersed organisations or people across the healthcare ecosystem before those changes are explicitly surfaced or discussed through other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential utility of the analysis.

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought a new challenge for general practice to deliver safe and effective care.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought a new challenge for general practice to deliver safe and effective care.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the pandemic's impact.

claim: The measures developed are presented as good measures of clinical activity in general practice.
source: The measures we have developed with our clinical advisory group are presented here as good measures of clinical activity in general practice and can be easily updated and monitored using our routinely updated dashboards on reports.opensafely.org, although we recommend that they should not be used in isolation as a sole measure of general practice activity.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the measures developed.

claim: The measures should not be used in isolation as a sole measure of general practice activity.
source: The measures we have developed with our clinical advisory group are presented here as good measures of clinical activity in general practice and can be easily updated and monitored using our routinely updated dashboards on reports.opensafely.org, although we recommend that they should not be used in isolation as a sole measure of general practice activity.
evidence: This is a recommendation from the authors.

claim: The measures can be expanded to include any measures needed to support NHS England's ambition to 'build back better' as we recover from the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: We can expand on these measures to include any measures needed to support NHS England's ambition to 'build back better' as we recover from the COVID-19 pandemic (DHSC/ONS/GAD/HO, 2020; NHS England, 2021a).
evidence: This is a claim about the potential for future work, supported by citations.

claim: The analysis can be updated regularly with extended follow-up time and further measures of activity using near-real time data to inform continued progress with NHS service restoration.
source: We can update this analysis regularly with extended follow-up time and further measures of activity such as measures defined by the Quality & Outcomes Framework (QOF) and the PINCER medication safety indicators (Fisher, 2023a; Avery et al., 2012) using near-real time data to inform continued progress with NHS service restoration.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential for future work, supported by citations.

claim: An extendable framework for assessing primary care activity and enabling monitoring of service recovery has been developed.
source: More broadly, we have developed an extendable framework for assessing primary care activity and enabling monitoring of service recovery.
evidence: This is a claim about the study's contribution.

claim: The framework allows fine-grained analysis over 58 million patient records.
source: This framework allows fine-grained analysis over 58 million patient records; analysis that is only possible as we have developed a modular system that allows for federated analytics, where all code written for data curation and analysis is written once, and executed in different locations containing different patients' data held by different providers.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the framework.

claim: Federated analytics across this scale of NHS EHR data is unprecedented.
source: Federated analytics across this scale of NHS EHR data is unprecedented.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach.

claim: The federated analytics approach is efficient because analyses can be easily updated, and expanded, because they are executed in a single framework from re-executable code.
source: This approach is efficient: analyses can be easily updated, and expanded, because they are executed in a single framework from re-executable code.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the approach.

claim: The federated analytics approach preserves patient trust.
source: It also preserves patient trust: OpenSAFELY was the single most highly trusted COVID-19 data project in a rigorous Citizens Jury sponsored by the NHS and the National Data Guardian (Malcolm Oswald, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a Citizens Jury report.

claim: OpenSAFELY was the single most highly trusted COVID-19 data project in a rigorous Citizens Jury sponsored by the NHS and the National Data Guardian.
source: OpenSAFELY was the single most highly trusted COVID-19 data project in a rigorous Citizens Jury sponsored by the NHS and the National Data Guardian (Malcolm Oswald, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a Citizens Jury report.

claim: Interactive 'point and click' infrastructure, OpenSAFELY-Interactive, has been developed to support delivery of dashboards.
source: We have also developed interactive 'point and click' infrastructure, OpenSAFELY-Interactive (https://interactive.opensafely.org/) to support delivery of dashboards and we are working with NHS England to make this tool available to approved users in order to perform their own similar analyses.
evidence: This describes a tool developed as part of the project.

claim: Work is underway with NHS England to make OpenSAFELY-Interactive available to approved users to perform their own similar analyses.
source: We have also developed interactive 'point and click' infrastructure, OpenSAFELY-Interactive (https://interactive.opensafely.org/) to support delivery of dashboards and we are working with NHS England to make this tool available to approved users in order to perform their own similar analyses.
evidence: This describes ongoing work.

claim: OpenSAFELY access is now available to users beyond the study group.
source: OpenSAFELY access is now available to users beyond our own group and we encourage others to use the OpenSAFELY platform and the framework presented here, to develop their own measures of clinical activity.
evidence: This describes the availability of the platform.

claim: There are plans to develop the functionality for individual practices to receive near real-time feedback on the measures presented.
source: We also plan to develop the functionality for individual practices to receive near real-time feedback on the measures presented here, informing their recovery of service.
evidence: This describes planned future work.

claim: Future research should include extending the monitoring of activity to more granular groups, such as those with long-term conditions.
source: We have previously highlighted important areas for future research following our work developing the OpenSAFELY SRO (Curtis et al., 2023). This includes extending the monitoring of activity to more granular groups, such as those with long-term conditions as well as assessing changes in activity in different demographic subgroups to assess health inequalities.
evidence: This describes planned future research, with citation to previous work.

claim: Future research should include assessing changes in activity in different demographic subgroups to assess health inequalities.
source: We have previously highlighted important areas for future research following our work developing the OpenSAFELY SRO (Curtis et al., 2023). This includes extending the monitoring of activity to more granular groups, such as those with long-term conditions as well as assessing changes in activity in different demographic subgroups to assess health inequalities.
evidence: This describes planned future research, with citation to previous work.

claim: OpenSAFELY can support follow up analyses on health inequalities and activity in specific patient groups.
source: OpenSAFELY can support these follow up analyses.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the platform.

claim: A successful secure open source software framework was delivered to describe trends and variation in clinical activity across an unprecedented scale of primary care data using federated analytics.
source: We successfully delivered a secure open source software framework to describe trends and variation in clinical activity across an unprecedented scale of primary care data using federated analytics.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's achievement.

claim: The changes in clinical activity will continue to be monitored using publicly available NHS OpenSAFELY SRO dashboards.
